name: Cooper Flagg
notes: Duke's consensus National Player of the Year and the rare ACC Player of the Year/Rookie of the Year in the same season (19.2/7.5/4.2, a 42-point freshman-scoring-record game, a Final Four run), the most complete, hyped freshman prospect in years. Dallas took him 1st. Flagg validated the hype immediately — 21.0/6.7/4.5 across all 70 starts, the youngest player ever to score 40+, the first teenager with a 50-point game, back-to-back 40-point games (first rookie since Iverson), unanimous Rookie of the Year. Hit: exactly the generational, franchise-cornerstone outcome projected, arriving on schedule.

name: Dylan Harper
notes: Rutgers's five-star, Morgan Wootten National Player of the Year freshman (19.4/4.6/4.0/1.4 stl, Third-Team All-Big Ten), elite lead-guard scoring and playmaking pedigree. San Antonio took him 2nd. Harper's role stayed measured in the regular season (11.8/3.4/3.9) but he broke out fully in a 23-game playoff run — 14.1/5.6/2.7, an 18 ppg Finals stretch in a loss to New York, All-Rookie First Team. Hit: real star-level talent that flashed its full ceiling once the games mattered most.

name: VJ Edgecombe
notes: Baylor's Big 12 Freshman of the Year (15.0/5.6/3.2/2.1 stl, Second-Team All-Big 12), elite two-way guard production and maturity. Philadelphia took him 3rd. Edgecombe delivered one of the best rookie debuts in years (34 points against Boston, third-most all-time for a debut) and sustained it across a full 75-start season — 16.0/5.6/4.2/1.4 stl, a 38-point/11-assist game, All-Rookie First Team. Hit: elite two-way college production translating immediately into a genuine star-level NBA rookie.

name: Kon Knueppel
notes: Duke's ACC Tournament MVP as a freshman (14.4/4.0/2.7 on elite 47.9/40.6/91.4% shooting, Wisconsin Mr. Basketball), elite shooting efficiency and feel. Charlotte took him 4th. Knueppel became the first rookie ever to lead the NBA in made three-pointers (273) across a full 80-start season — 18.5/5.3/3.4 on 47.5/42.5% shooting, runner-up Rookie of the Year to Flagg, All-Rookie First Team. Hit: elite shooting efficiency that became a genuine, historically productive rookie NBA scorer.

name: Ace Bailey
notes: Rutgers's highest-ranked recruit ever and Third-Team All-Big Ten freshman (17.6/7.2/1.3, a 39-point game against Indiana), elite scoring and size upside from a five-star recruit. Utah took him 5th. Bailey started immediately (61 of 72 games, 13.8/4.2/1.8, a 32-point game, All-Rookie Second Team), becoming the youngest Jazz player ever to reach 500 career points. Solid outcome: real recruiting-era scoring talent translating into a genuine, productive young NBA starter, short of top-five star trajectory so far.

name: Tre Johnson
notes: Texas's SEC Freshman of the Year (19.9/3.1/2.7 on 39.7% from three, Second-Team All-SEC, a 39-point game breaking Kevin Durant's Texas freshman record), elite volume scoring pedigree. Washington took him 6th. Johnson debuted with the franchise's best rookie scoring debut since 1992 (16 points) and settled into a real, sustained scoring role (12.2/2.8/2.0 across 42 starts, 35.8% from three). Solid outcome: real scoring talent translating into a genuine, productive NBA rookie shooter.

name: Jeremiah Fears
notes: A one-and-done Oklahoma four-star and the school's fourth top-seven pick in 16 years (17.1/4.1/4.1, first true freshman since Trae Young with a 30-point game, a Battle 4 Atlantis title run), elite lead-guard scoring instincts. New Orleans took him 7th. Fears became the first Pelicans rookie ever to play all 82 games (14.3/3.7/3.4, a franchise-rookie-record 40-point game), All-Rookie Second Team. Hit: real lead-guard scoring pedigree translating into a genuine, durable NBA rookie starter.

name: Egor Dёmin
notes: A Real Madrid academy product and two-time EuroLeague Next Generation Tournament champion (26 points/11 rebounds in the 2024 final) who became BYU's first-ever five-star recruit (10.6/5.5/3.9/1.2 stl as a freshman, Big 12 All-Freshman), elite international pedigree and playmaking feel. Brooklyn took him 8th. Dëmin broke the NBA rookie record for consecutive games with a made three (34 straight) and started 45 of 52 games (10.3/3.3/3.2) before plantar fasciitis ended his season in March 2026; a strong 2026 Summer League (21/4.3, ESPN's Best Sophomore) suggested real continued growth. Solid outcome: elite feel and shooting translating into a genuine rookie starter role, injury the interruption.

name: Collin Murray-Boyles
notes: South Carolina's Second-Team All-SEC sophomore breakout (16.8/8.3/1.3 blk after battling mononucleosis as a freshman), real, efficient positionless production. Toronto took him 9th. Murray-Boyles's rookie regular season stayed modest (8.5/5.0 on 57.9% shooting across 22 starts) before a real playoff breakout — 14.4/6.4 on an elite 65.6% shooting across seven games — earning All-Rookie Second Team honors. Hit: real efficient college production that flashed genuine star-level upside once the postseason arrived.

name: Khaman Maluach
notes: A 7'1", 7'6.75"-wingspan Duke freshman and the highest-drafted player ever from NBA Academy Africa/the Basketball Africa League (8.6/6.6/1.3 blk on an elite 71.2% FG, ACC All-Freshman, BAL rebounding leader), elite rim-running and shot-blocking upside. Houston took him 10th (traded to Phoenix in a seven-team Kevin Durant-return deal). Maluach's rookie role stayed limited (3.0/2.9 in 8.9 minutes across 46 games) before his first NBA start produced a real flash (4 points, 14 rebounds, 3 blocks). Mixed outcome: elite physical tools still finding real NBA minutes behind a crowded roster.

name: Cedric Coward
notes: An unusually well-traveled path from Division III Willamette to Eastern Washington (First-Team All-Big Sky) to Washington State, where a season-ending shoulder injury cut short a strong 17.7 ppg lead-scorer stretch, real late-emerging efficient scoring on an incomplete final sample. Portland took him 11th (traded to Memphis for the rights to Yang Hansen). Coward delivered immediately — a 27-point, 6-for-6-from-three debut-week game, the first rookie in franchise history to go perfect from deep, All-Rookie First Team (13.6/5.9/2.8 across 47 starts). Hit: real late-blooming efficiency that became an immediate, genuine NBA rookie contributor.

name: Noa Essengue
notes: A French forward who developed through Centre Fédéral and Germany's Ratiopharm Ulm, becoming a key Bundesliga contributor as a teenager, real long-term two-way upside from a proven European pathway. Chicago took him 12th. Essengue's rookie season was wiped out almost entirely by a shoulder injury requiring surgery (2 games, 3 minutes total) after a brief, strong G League flash (23.0/8.5). Bust so far: real developmental upside that a serious shoulder injury has kept from any real NBA opportunity.

name: Derik Queen
notes: Maryland's Big Ten Freshman of the Year and First-Team All-Big Ten (16.5/9.0/1.9, a 31-point Big Ten Tournament semifinal, a signature game-winning shot), elite, efficient (52.6% FG) interior scoring and passing for a big man, weak shooting range (20% from three) the flag. Atlanta took him 13th (traded to New Orleans). A wrist ligament tear requiring surgery cost him Summer League and part of camp, but Queen still played 81 games (48 starts) and delivered a historic rookie season — the first rookie center ever with a 30-point triple-double, a 30/22 season finale, All-Rookie Second Team (11.7/7.1/3.7). Hit: elite college scoring and passing translating directly into a genuine, historically productive rookie big man.

name: Carter Bryant
notes: A consensus four-star Arizona freshman whose limited role (6.5/4.1/1.0 blk on 46.0/37.1% shooting) undersold real defensive-forward and shooting upside. San Antonio took him 14th. Bryant's rookie role stayed marginal (4.2/2.5, no starts across 71 games) with real playoff minutes (2.6/1.7 across 22 games) — a runner-up finish in the 2026 Slam Dunk Contest signaled real athletic upside. Bust relative to a first-round slot so far, though real flashes and a durable, deep rookie role on a contender.

name: Thomas Sorber
notes: A one-and-done Georgetown center and Third-Team All-Big East freshman (14.5/8.5/2.4, a historic first Georgetown player drafted straight from his freshman year), real, immediate two-way big-man production. Oklahoma City took him 15th. A torn ACL suffered in an offseason workout in September 2025 wiped out his entire rookie season before it began. Bust so far: elite, ready-made college production that a serious knee injury has kept entirely from NBA opportunity.

name: Yang Hansen
notes: A CBA veteran (Qingdao Eagles) who won back-to-back Rookie of the Year/Defensive Player of the Year and then All-CBA First Team honors (16.6/10.5/3.0 in his second pro season), the third-highest Chinese draft pick ever with real, proven professional production well beyond his draft-year peers. Memphis took him 16th (traded to Portland for the rights to Cedric Coward). Hansen's rookie NBA role stayed marginal (2.2/1.5 across 43 games, mostly G League time). Bust so far at the NBA level, despite a genuinely accomplished pre-draft professional résumé.

name: Joan Beringer
notes: A remarkably late basketball starter (age 14-15) who developed rapidly through SIG Strasbourg and Slovenia's Cedevita Olimpija (a Slovenian Cup title as a rookie pro), real, fast-improving rim-protecting upside on thin direct stats. Minnesota took him 17th. Beringer's rookie role stayed limited (3.9/2.3/0.7 blk in 7.9 minutes across 40 games) but flashed real long-term upside — a 24-point/12-rebound/7-block double-double in the season finale. Mixed outcome: thin rookie minutes concealing a real, rapidly-developing shot-blocking talent.

name: Walter Clayton
notes: An Iona-to-Florida riser and consensus First-Team All-American senior who led Florida to the 2025 national title (18.3/4.2/3.7, Final Four Most Outstanding Player, SEC Male Athlete of the Year), elite, proven winning production from an experienced college path. Washington took him 18th (traded to Utah). Clayton's early Jazz role was modest (6.8/2.0/5.5) before a February 2026 trade to Memphis (part of the Jaren Jackson Jr. deal) unlocked real production — 9.7/5.7 across 24 games. Solid outcome: real winning college pedigree translating into a genuine, growing NBA role after a trade.

name: Nolan Traoré
notes: A French guard who developed through Centre Fédéral and a brief Saint-Quentin stint, including a record 45-point game against Barcelona at the 2024 Adidas Next Generation Tournament, real long-term point-guard upside from a lottery-caliber international profile. Brooklyn took him 19th. Traoré earned real rookie minutes (8.9/3.8/1.8 across 31 starts in 56 games on modest 38.0/31.8% shooting) before a December 2025 G League assignment. Solid outcome: real developmental point-guard talent given genuine rookie-year NBA opportunity, efficiency the ongoing swing skill.

name: Kasparas Jakučionis
notes: A FC Barcelona academy product (a EuroLeague debut at 17) who became a Second-Team All-Big Ten Illinois freshman (15.0 ppg, a 13-assist game in just his second college game), elite feel and pedigree from a rare dual college-and-EuroLeague path. Miami took him 20th. Jakučionis's rookie role stayed modest (6.2/2.6/2.6 across 53 games, some G League time on strong 42.9/42.3% shooting) before a July 2026 blockbuster trade to Milwaukee (the Giannis deal). Solid outcome: real feel and shooting efficiency in a limited rookie role, now with a fresh opportunity.

name: Amari Williams
notes: Grad transfer big (four years at Drexel, one at Kentucky) who entered the draft as a defense-and-processing prospect: 7'0" with a 7'5" wingspan, a three-time CAA Defensive Player of the Year, an excellent passer and rebounder (10.9/8.5/3.2 at 56.1% FG as a senior), but not a shooter and light on lateral quickness — concerns evaluators flagged as the swing factor for whether his defense would translate to NBA speed. Boston took him 46th overall. As scouted, the NBA opportunity hasn't come yet — buried behind Neemias Queta and Luka Garza, then further blocked by the midseason Nikola Vucevic trade, he played just 22 games (6.6 min, 1.4/1.8/0.5). The signal is in the G League tape instead: 18 games with Maine at 17.8/10.9/4.9 with 1.8 blk on 57.3% shooting — the passing and rebounding translate cleanly, the question is still whether the feet hold up against NBA ball-handlers. No outcome tag yet; too early, and the G League run is more informative than the NBA minutes so far.
